summary: Defines a new 6LoWPAN dispatch type for route-over networks. It first targets compression of RPL data packet information: the RPL Option and the source routing header, plus an IP-in-IP technique. It can be extended for other uses. Later RFCs update it.

eli5.summary: Tiny sensors send very small messages. This is a shorthand for the extra routing notes on each message so they fit in less space.

questions: how does rpl header compression work
subtitle: A compact way to carry RPL routing information in tiny 6LoWPAN frames.

tldr.problem: Low-power wireless links such as IEEE 802.15.4 allow only 127 bytes per frame, yet RPL needs an 8-byte hop-by-hop option, source routing headers and sometimes IP-in-IP encapsulation on packets.
tldr.mechanism: A new 6LoWPAN Routing Header (6LoRH) dispatch in Page 1 carries compressed forms of the source routing header, the RPL Packet Information and the IP-in-IP outer header, each as a small type-based header placed before LOWPAN_IPHC.
tldr.outcome: Packets shrink, which saves energy and avoids fragmentation, but the scheme expects a homogeneous network and consumed source route entries are not recoverable. Later RFCs update it.

today: RFC 8138 is a Proposed Standard from April 2017 and is updated by RFC 9008, RFC 9035 and RFC 9914. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Routing Headers Need Compression
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) are designed around saving energy, and sending less data is one way to do it. On the classical IEEE 802.15.4 physical layer a frame is limited to 127 bytes, far below the IPv6 minimum MTU of 1280 bytes. RFC 6282 already compresses IPv6 headers for these networks.

RPL routing adds more. Its RPL Packet Information (RPI) normally rides in a Hop-by-Hop header that takes 8 bytes, while the RPI payload usually needs only 19 bits. In Non-Storing mode a source routing header (SRH) is also needed for packets going down the graph. Because the original packet must not be tampered with, inserting or removing such headers at a router means wrapping the packet in an extra IP-in-IP encapsulation.

This RFC extends the 6lo adaptation layer so these routing artifacts can be compressed, and it is extensible for other formats.
sections.eli5: Messages in tiny sensor networks must fit in a very small envelope. The routing notes were taking up too much room, so this shortens them.

sections.title: Page 1 Dispatch and Header Placement
sections.content:
The 6LoRH works inside Page 1 of the 6LoWPAN Paging Dispatch (RFC 8025), selected by the dispatch value 11110001. It is expressed as a Type-Length-Value field, so it can grow in the future, and it uses the bit pattern 10xxxxxx. A router that does not recognize the format is expected to drop the packet.

Placement rules are strict. A 6LoRH MUST come after any Fragmentation or Mesh header and MUST come before the LOWPAN_IPHC, so adding or removing it never changes the part of the packet encoded by LOWPAN_IPHC. Chains of headers MUST be compressed in the same order as in the uncompressed packet, the compressed IP-in-IP header is placed last in its chain, and compressed SRH entries MUST come before the compressed RPI.
sections.eli5: The shorthand notes go in a fixed spot on the message, after the postage and before the main address, so the main address never has to change.

sections.title: General Format and Address Compression
sections.content:
6LoRH comes in two forms. An Elective header (101xxxxx) can be skipped if not understood and carries a Length in bytes, excluding the first 2 bytes. A Critical header (100xxxxx) cannot be ignored: a node that does not support its Type MUST silently discard the packet. Its Type-Specific Extension (TSE) field means different things for different types. Each form has its own Type registry.

Addresses are compressed by choosing a reference with a long prefix match and removing the matching part. To expand, the receiver overwrites the N rightmost bytes of the reference address with the compressed bytes, which the RFC calls coalescence. The reference is often the root of the RPL DODAG. For a Global RPLInstanceID the root can be found from the RPL instance, while for a Local Instance the root address MUST be explicit.
sections.eli5: Some notes can be ignored if you do not understand them, and others must be understood or the message is thrown away. To shorten an address, you drop the part both sides already know.

sections.title: The Source Routing Header, Compressed
sections.content:
The SRH-6LoRH is a Critical header that compresses the RPL source routing header. It holds the hops of a route, ordered from first to last. All addresses in one header are compressed the same way, and Types 0 to 4 give lengths of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 bytes. The Size field is the number of hops minus 1, up to a maximum of 32 hops per header, and several headers may follow one another for more hops or different compression levels. The header length is 2 + address length * (Size + 1) bytes.

Unlike the uncompressed form, there is no swapping of addresses. A router that finds its own address in the first entry pops it before forwarding, so the packet shrinks along the path. The RFC accepts that the routing information is lost along the way, arguing that the energy savings outweigh the value of reversing a routing header. If strict source routing is enforced and the router is not the segment endpoint, it MUST drop the packet.
sections.eli5: It is like a list of stops on a trip. Each stop crosses itself off the list as the message passes, so the list gets shorter and lighter as it goes.

sections.title: The RPL Packet Information Header
sections.content:
The RPI-6LoRH is a Critical header of Type 5 that carries the RPI. The RPI has an O, an R and an F bit, an 8-bit RPLInstanceID and a 16-bit SenderRank. Two flags describe the compression. When I is set, the RPLInstanceID is elided and is the Global RPLInstanceID 0. When K is set, the SenderRank is compressed to 1 byte by eliding the least significant byte, which works when MinHopRankIncrease is a multiple of 256. Otherwise the SenderRank takes 2 bytes.

The result is four possible layouts, from the most compressed (I=1, K=1) to the least (I=0, K=0). A non-RPL router that receives it should drop the packet rather than skip it, to avoid loops from reinjecting it in the wrong RPL Instance.
sections.eli5: The little tag saying which game and what rank a message belongs to is squeezed down, and if the answer is the usual one, it is left out completely.

sections.title: The IP-in-IP Header
sections.content:
The IP-in-IP-6LoRH is an Elective header of Type 6 that compresses the outer IPv6 header of an encapsulation. It is needed so that a router that inserts a field, and is not the packet's source, can be named in case of an error. Its Length MUST be at least 1, for a Hop Limit that is decremented at each hop, and the packet is dropped when it reaches 0.

If the Length is exactly 1, the Encapsulator Address is elided, meaning it is a well-known router such as the RPL root. A longer Length means a compressed encapsulator address follows, for example a Length of 3 means a 2-byte address. Removing the RPI to leave the domain can be done by dropping the RPI-6LoRH, so an IP-in-IP header is not needed for that alone.
sections.eli5: When a helper adds a note to someone else's message, it wraps it in an outer envelope with the helper's name. The shorthand makes that envelope tiny, or leaves the name out if everyone knows it.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
The design expects a homogeneous network where all nodes, or none, use this compression. It has no way to learn at forwarding time whether the next hop supports it, and it does not try to provide backward compatibility. Mismatches are treated as administrative errors.

A node that expected a 6LoRH and found none, or received one it does not recognize, is expected to send a rate-limited ICMPv6 Parameter Problem message (type 4) to the root, with code 0 or code 1 respectively. It SHOULD NOT use a 6LoRH in that message, and it should raise a management alert.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the network must speak the same shorthand. If someone does not, the message is dropped and a note goes to the boss so a person can fix the setup.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4944, RFC 6282 and RFC 6553 apply. The compressed format is logically equivalent to the in-line format and is believed not to create a new threat compared to RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 6554.

One caveat is that consumed hops are removed from the SRH, but a node may still detect that the rest of a source-routed path includes a loop. The RFC adds that if an attacker is not part of the loop, some node at the beginning of the loop can detect and remove it.
sections.eli5: Using shorthand does not open a new door for attackers, and the older safety rules still apply.

fields.name: K
fields.desc: Set when the SenderRank is compressed to 1 byte.
